concept.name: Black-Scholes model
concept.definition: The Black-Scholes model is a continuous-time option-pricing framework that values a European option by constructing a continuously rebalanced, riskless hedge between the option and its underlying, yielding a partial differential equation whose solution is the Black-Scholes formula. Published by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes in 1973, with Robert Merton's concurrent mathematical extension, it assumes geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility, a constant risk-free rate, no dividends, and frictionless markets.
concept.intuition: If you can perfectly cancel an option's risk by holding the right amount of stock, the hedged portfolio must earn the risk-free rate — and that single requirement pins down the option's fair price, whatever investors expect the stock to do.
concept.mechanics: The formula prices a European call as S*N(d1) - K*e^(-rT)*N(d2), with d1, d2 functions of spot, strike, rate, volatility, and time. Its practical legacy is twofold: the Greeks (closed-form hedge parameters) and implied volatility — the model is routinely inverted to quote option prices as volatilities rather than used as a literal price predictor.
concept.formula: C = S*N(d1) - K*e^(-rT)*N(d2); P = K*e^(-rT)*N(-d2) - S*N(-d1); d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)T] / (sigma*sqrt(T)); d2 = d1 - sigma*sqrt(T).
concept.failure_modes: Constant-volatility lognormality is empirically false: returns have fat tails and skew, so the model systematically underprices crash protection (the post-1987 volatility smile) and gap risk breaks the continuous-hedging argument. Its inputs — especially future volatility — are unobservable, making the output only as good as the guess.
concept.misconceptions: The model does not assume markets are efficient or that it predicts prices; it is a relative-pricing consistency device. Nor is implied volatility from the model a forecast — it is the market's price of insurance expressed in the model's units.
